events.name: Earth forms
q: usgs-age-earth
These calculations result in an age for the Earth and meteorites, and hence the Solar System, of 4.54 billion years with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent.
climate-gov-hottest
Following the collision that spawned the Moon, the planet was estimated to have been around 2,300 Kelvin (3,680°F).

events.name: Early atmosphere and oceans
q: climate-gov-coldest
Carbon dioxide was anywhere from 10 to 2,500 times present levels, and methane may have been as much as 10,000 times higher than present levels. Atmospheric oxygen was virtually nonexistent.
nps-precambrian
Life first appeared on Earth during the Archean Eon.

events.name: Faint young Sun
q: nasa-faint-young-sun

Three billion years ago, the young Sun was 70% as bright as it is today. Under these dimmer conditions, Earth should have been frozen solid. Yet geological evidence shows stable liquid water already existed long before that.

events.name: Great Oxidation Event
events.dateText: some 2.4 billion years ago; “between 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago”
q: nasa-astrobio-goe-2021
the 'Great Oxidation Event,' when a rise in atmospheric oxygen altered the environment and the biosphere of our planet some 2.4 billion years ago.
nasa-astrobio-whiffs-2023
What is known as the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) occurred sometime between 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago, leaving the atmosphere rich in oxygen.
events.o2: not reliably quantified in the sources read

events.name: Huronian ice ages
q: climate-gov-coldest
At least one of them constituted what geologists call a Snowball Earth event, when the planet's surface was entirely, or almost entirely, frozen.
climate-gov-coldest
Evidence suggests these glaciations reached equatorial regions at sea level.

events.name: Snowball Earth (Cryogenian)
events.dateText: Sturtian about 720–660 Ma; Marinoan about 640–635 Ma
q: climate-gov-coldest
Geologists have identified two glaciations during the Neoproterozoic: the Sturtian (about 720 to 660 million years ago) and the Marinoan (about 640 to 635 million years ago).
climate-gov-coldest
But just how complete the Neoproterozoic ice coverage was—whether it was a Snowball Earth or a Slushball Earth—remains an area of active research.
events.finding: Climate.gov gives the deep-freeze window as “between 750 and 600 million years ago” in one article and “between 600 and 800 million years ago” in another; the time scale has the Cryogenian at ~720–~635 Ma.

events.name: Cambrian explosion
q: nps-cambrian
an evolutionary burst of animal origins dating from 545 to 525 million years ago.
nps-cambrian
During Cambrian time, life was only common in the water. The land was barren
events.temp: not reliably quantified in the sources read

events.name: End-Ordovician extinction
q: nps-mass-extinctions
related to an episode of rapid glaciation and its abrupt retreat on the supercontinent Gondwana… The glaciation lowered global sea level
events.loss: about 86% of species, 57% of genera, and 27% of taxonomic families

events.name: Late Devonian extinction
events.dateText: about 372 million years ago (most critical event)
q: nps-mass-extinctions
not very clear… global cooling, volcanic activity, an impact by a comet or other extraterrestrial object, and an overabundance of nutrients
events.loss: 75% of species, 35% of genera, and 19% of taxonomic families

events.name: Pangaea
events.dateText: assembled by the Pennsylvanian–Permian; breakup began about 225–200 Ma
q: nps-permian
During the Permian Period, Earth's crustal plates formed a single, massive continent called Pangaea.
usgs-dynamic-earth
According to the continental drift theory, the supercontinent Pangaea began to break up about 225-200 million years ago, eventually fragmenting into the continents as we know them today.

events.name: End-Permian extinction
q: nps-mass-extinctions
Massive volcanic eruptions of flood basalts in Siberia are thought to be the triggering cause
usgs-siberian-traps-2017

The most biologically severe of the extinction events, which occurred at the end of the Permian Period (about 252 million years ago), is thought to have been triggered by greenhouses gases generated from the Siberian Traps LIP, which erupted at the same time.
events.loss: 96% of species, 56% of genera, and 57% of taxonomic families
events.finding: NPS’s Permian page gives “95% of all species” and 53 % of families; its mass-extinction page gives 96 % and 57 %. The NPS time-scale graphic dates the boundary 252.2 Ma; USGS and ICS 251.9.

events.name: End-Triassic extinction
q: nps-mass-extinctions
The major cause is thought to have been the opening of the Atlantic Ocean as the supercontinent Pangea broke up
events.loss: an estimated 80% of species, 47% of genera, and 23% taxonomic families

events.name: Cretaceous hot greenhouse
q: climate-gov-hottest
One spike was the Cretaceous Hot Greenhouse roughly 92 million years ago, about 25 million years before Earth's last dinosaurs went extinct.
climate-gov-hottest
Temperatures were so high that champsosaurs (crocodile-like reptiles) lived as far north as the Canadian Arctic, and warm-temperature forests thrived near the South Pole.
events.co2: not reliably quantified in the sources read
events.finding: The same Climate.gov article dates the Cretaceous Hothouse “roughly 92 million years ago” in the text and “100 million years ago” in a caption.

events.name: End-Cretaceous extinction (Chicxulub)
q: nps-mass-extinctions
An asteroid impact that formed the Chicxulub crater in the Yucatan caused instantaneous climate change and plunged Earth into darkness.
events.loss: 76% of species, 40% of genera, and 17% of taxonomic families
events.finding: NPS gives the asteroid as 10–20 km across with a crater nearly 190 km wide on one page, and “probably 6 to 10 miles across” with a structure “more than 90 miles across” on another. A 2017 USGS release says “about 65 million years ago”.

events.name: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
q: climate-gov-hottest
During the PETM, the global mean temperature appears to have risen by as much as 5-8°C (9-14°F) to an average temperature as high as 34°C (93°F).
climate-gov-hottest
a massive release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, at least doubling or possibly even quadrupling the background concentrations.
inglis-2020
the average GMST estimate (66 % confidence) during the latest Paleocene, PETM, and EECO was 26.3 °C (22.3 to 28.3 °C), 31.6 °C (27.2 to 34.5 °C), and 27.0 °C (23.2 to 29.7 °C), respectively.
events.finding: Climate.gov’s article says “about 6°C” warming in one place and “as much as 5-8°C” in another.

events.name: Antarctic ice sheet forms
q: hutchinson-2021

The Eocene–Oligocene transition (EOT) was a climate shift from a largely ice-free greenhouse world to an icehouse climate, involving the first major glaciation of Antarctica and global cooling occurring ∼34 million years ago (Ma) and lasting ∼790 kyr.
hutchinson-2021

The two principal suggested explanations of this transition are a decline in atmospheric CO₂ and changes to ocean gateways, while orbital forcing likely influenced the precise timing of the glaciation.
events.co2: a decrease of ca. 40 % (∼325 ppm drop) — “should be considered an upper estimate”

events.name: Pleistocene ice ages
q: climate-gov-coldest
In fact, we are technically still in an ice age. We're just living out our lives during an interglacial.
climate-gov-coldest
they waxed and waned over timescales of about 20,000 to 100,000 years, due partly to Milankovitch Cycles.

events.name: Last Glacial Maximum
q: climate-gov-coldest
The latest ice age peaked about 20,000 years ago, when global temperatures were likely about 10°F (5°C) colder than today.
nps-quaternary
With so much water locked up in the form of ice, sea level dropped to about 430 feet (130 m) below current levels.
events.sea: about 125 m (USGS), about 120 m (NOAA, regional page), about 130 m (NPS, Pleistocene generally)

events.name: Holocene
q: nps-quaternary
Marked climatic warming and the disappearance of the continental glaciers mark the transition between the Pleistocene and Holocene.
ncei-paleo-context-2022
The Mid-Holocene Warm Period, observed about 6,000 years ago, was generally warmer than today during summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

events.name: Industrial era
q: climate-gov-hottest
Since 1850, global surface temperatures have risen roughly 0.11°F (0.06°C) per decade. Since 1982, they have risen 0.36°F (0.20°C) per decade.

usgs.note: The Anthropocene currently has no formal status in the Divisions of Geologic Time and is not recognized by the GNC.

ics.caveat: Numerical ages are subject to ongoing revision and do not define units in the Phanerozoic and the Ediacaran; only GSSPs do.

proxies.def: These proxy data are preserved physical characteristics of the environment that can stand in for direct measurements.
items: These layers contain dust, air bubbles, or isotopes of oxygen, differing from year to year based on the surrounding environment, that can be used to interpret the past climate of an area.
Scientists drill cores of the sediments from the basin floors and examine their contents, which include tiny fossils and chemicals, to interpret past climates.
Because climate conditions influence tree growth, patterns in tree-ring widths, density, and isotopic composition reflect variations in climate.
The carbonate also contains isotopes of oxygen as well as trace metals that can be used to determine the temperature of the water in which the coral grew.
Scientists can then make inferences about the climate of the area based on the types of plants found in each layer.
Because the amount of water making its way into caves determines the amount speleothems grow, their layers can indicate times of both heavy precipitation and drought.
For example, scientists used historical grape harvest dates to reconstruct summer temperatures, between April and September, in Paris from 1370 to 1879.

isotope.q: the relative concentrations of oxygen isotopes in ice cores (at high latitudes, precipitation in colder conditions has a lower O-18/O-16 ratio as compared to warmer conditions).

tradeoff.q: Typically, records that have large timespans have less detail about short-term climate changes, while shorter records are often more detailed.
